chapters.title: Depth without a map
chapters.body: Foreground branches, distant trunks and pools of light give Ori's woodland several visual layers. The playable path occupies only part of that space. What remains beyond reach matters too: it suggests a forest continuing outside the player's route, larger than the immediate challenge on screen.

chapters.title: Movement makes a landscape
chapters.body: New abilities change how familiar branches and gaps can be read. A barrier becomes an invitation to return, and a remembered corner acquires another use. Moon Studios makes exploration a changing relationship with place: the forest remains recognisable while the player's way of inhabiting it grows.

chapters.title: Breath measures distance
chapters.body: An oxygen reserve changes the meaning of a short swim. Distance must be considered together with the return journey, and curiosity has to leave room for retreat. Subnautica turns a basic bodily need into a way of reading space: every expedition carries its own invisible boundary.

chapters.title: A window below the surface
chapters.body: An underwater base changes the ocean from a place crossed into a place watched. A window separates shelter from open water without removing their closeness. The scene encourages a different kind of attention: staying still long enough to notice movement that an urgent journey would miss.

chapters.title: The island as a page
chapters.body: Myst often leaves a mechanism waiting without immediately explaining its purpose. A symbol seen elsewhere or a detail recorded in a notebook may change its meaning. Reading here is an active practice: the player assembles connections between places that the screen never presents all at once.

chapters.title: An invitation to doubt
chapters.body: The voices encountered through Myst's books do not remove the need for judgement. Listening also means weighing a claim against the world around it. Rand Miller's adventure makes the reader responsible for interpretation: an account can be compelling without being sufficient evidence for the choice ahead.

chapters.body: In Outer Wilds, an important discovery can be an explanation rather than a new tool. A familiar location becomes approachable differently because the player understands more about it. game.Name: Pac-Man
game.Overview:
Pac-Man is a maze-chase arcade game with single-player and alternating two-player modes. The player controls Pac-Man, a yellow circular character who must navigate an enclosed maze while eating small dots scattered along its paths. The objective in each stage is to clear the maze of all dots while avoiding four ghosts that pursue Pac-Man through the corridors. As the player progresses, the maze layout remains the same, but the game becomes more difficult as ghost behavior, speed, and vulnerability periods change. The maze also includes side tunnels that connect the left and right edges of the screen. These tunnels can be used to escape danger, as ghosts move more slowly through them than Pac-Man.

The four ghosts each follow distinct movement patterns that affect how they chase the player. Blinky, the red ghost, tends to pursue Pac-Man directly. Pinky, the pink ghost, attempts to position itself ahead of Pac-Man. Inky, the blue ghost, uses a more complex pattern based partly on Pac-Man’s position and Blinky’s location, making its movement less predictable. Clyde, the orange ghost, alternates between approaching Pac-Man and moving away or patrolling. Their movement also alternates between periods of pursuit and brief scatter phases, during which they retreat toward different corners of the maze before resuming the chase. Contact with any ghost while it is dangerous costs Pac-Man a life, and the game ends when all lives are lost.

chapters.title: The race puts the disc to work
chapters.body: Spooling loaded new data as Crash moved forward or back. Jason Rubin recalls Kelly Flock asking how many CD accesses finishing the game might require: Andy Gavin estimated roughly 120,000 offhand; Flock cited a 70,000 rating for the drive and continued supporting the project. These are remembered conversational estimates, not failure measurements: they reveal the technical ambition behind that densely detailed world.

chapters.title: A face inside a grid
chapters.body: Moustache, cap and overalls become a signature, but they also solve the problem of making a body readable in a few pixels. The moustache defines the face, the cap simplifies the hair and the overalls distinguish arms from torso. Miyamoto turns a graphical constraint into personality. Before becoming an icon, Mario must make his actions immediately understandable.

game.Name: Donkey Kong
game.Overview:
Donkey Kong is a fixed-screen platform game in which the player controls a carpenter originally identified as Jumpman and later known as Mario. Donkey Kong has carried away a woman called Lady, later named Pauline, and taken her to the top of a construction site. Mario must run across platforms, climb ladders, and jump over hazards to reach her before the decreasing bonus counter reaches zero.

The arcade game contains four distinct screen designs, identified as heights of 25, 50, 75, and 100 meters. On the first, Mario climbs a series of sloping girders while Donkey Kong rolls barrels down from above. Some barrels travel down ladders or strike an oil drum at the bottom of the screen, producing fireballs that pursue Mario. Hammers found along the route can temporarily destroy barrels and fireballs, but Mario swings them automatically and cannot jump or climb ladders until their effect expires.

chapters.title: Every path can hide another
chapters.body: In 1990, Super Mario World accompanies the Super Famicom's Japanese debut. Miyamoto and Nintendo's team retain the immediate pleasure of jumping but give it a more branching geography: secret exits, alternative routes and a partnership with Yoshi. The world does more than connect levels. It promises hidden possibilities and invites us back to places we thought we had finished.

chapters.title: The jump finds a third dimension
chapters.body: Super Mario 64 needs more than depth in the scenery: players must orient a body, a viewpoint and an intention. The lawn outside the castle becomes a place to experiment, turn and climb. Under Miyamoto's direction, a familiar Mario carries a new grammar. The pleasure of movement comes before the objective, making space something to discover with our hands.

chapters.title: A world held in your hands
chapters.body: The Game Boy came from the development group led by Gunpei Yokoi, not from a Miyamoto invention. Its place in Nintendo's history still shows how the company's work depends on intersecting skills: hardware, software, characters and everyday habits. Taking play beyond the living room means designing for hands, light, batteries and short intervals. Authorship remains part of a collective culture able to continue beyond one name.

chapters.title: Honouring a way of making us play
chapters.body: In 2010 BAFTA awarded Miyamoto its Fellowship, its highest individual honour. It recognised a career that made actions such as jumping, exploring and trying again familiar to millions. The award celebrates a creative path without erasing the teams that made it possible. Authorship in games can also be measured through the actions entrusted to the audience.

chapters.title: Before the melody everyone knows
chapters.body: Koji Kondo joins Nintendo in 1984. Before his name becomes inseparable from Mario and Zelda, he is a young sound specialist in a team learning new ways to work. Devil World is an early workshop. Music gains its own place in design: more than an effect to program, it is a sensibility working alongside pictures and movement.

game.Name: Devil World
game.Overview: Lost in the maze of Devil World, Tamagon the Dragon has to steer clear of the Devil, his nasty co-Devils, and his treacherous helpers, Medaman, the Fried-Eggman and Bon-Bon, and ward off their attacks by breathing fire. After each round, the maze scrolls up, down, right or left. The Devil decides the direction and points with his finger. As you guide Tamagon through the maze, you also have to avoid being sandwiched between the walls.

chapters.title: A score beneath your fingers
chapters.body: Blue skies are not enough. The first idea for Super Mario Bros.' ground theme suggested a relaxed stroll, but Mario ran and jumped. Kondo had to listen to the character, not simply look at the scenery. The finished melody seems to belong to our fingers. Through acceleration, pauses and restarts, music helps us feel movement before we can explain it.

chapters.title: Music makes room for the journey
chapters.body: A melody accompanies repeated returns: we cross a field, a village or a doorway again. Koji Kondo works with repetition without reducing the world to a motionless refrain. In Zelda, sound can suggest an emotional direction, then leave room for the landscape to keep speaking.

chapters.title: When the player becomes a musician
chapters.body: Ocarina of Time places an instrument in Link's hands and its gestures on the controller. Remembering a short sequence lets us affect the world: music becomes an ability to use. Kondo's work meets the player's memory, inviting us to take part in the performance rather than simply listen.

chapters.title: The instruments change, the gesture remains
chapters.body: From the Famicom's spare sound to Super Mario Galaxy's orchestral possibilities, more than the range of timbres changes: so does teamwork. Other voices emerge alongside Kondo, including Mahito Yokota. His legacy is not a formula to repeat but a question to pass on: how can music meet what the player is doing? The piano is a starting point; the game is where the answer comes alive.

chapters.title: Before the labyrinth, a sheet of paper
chapters.body: On a dungeon plan, each room is first a position relative to other rooms. Paper makes routes, returns and places to remember visible: what becomes discovery on screen begins as a relationship to design. Nintendo's preserved development documents reveal this handmade side of the original Zelda. The player's mystery begins with someone carefully arranging what we cannot yet see.

chapters.title: Before the landscape came a square
chapters.body: Graph-paper plans preserve the world before it starts moving. Ground, pipes and obstacles occupy positions that must become instructions for the program. They reveal a level as an editable composition of measurements and revisions. A drawing cannot establish whether a sequence works: it has to be played. Between the paper and the controller, the design finally meets the player's sense of time.
chapters.image_title: Super Mario Bros.: original course planning reproduced in Nintendo's Super Mario Maker booklet.

chapters.title: The music has to know how to run
chapters.body: Koji Kondo recalled that an early piece inspired by the scenery's sky and greenery did not match Mario's rhythm. The task was more than describing a pleasant place: it had to accompany a body running and jumping. The music's character emerges from that relationship. Its melody is memorable partly because it seems to understand our hands, allowing action and listening to belong to the same experience.

chapters.title: A save with its own screen
chapters.body: The VMU could display information while seated in the controller and, in supported games, carry small experiences away from the television. Saving was no longer its only visible role. The accessory suggested a relationship between screens, letting a fragment of a larger game acquire its own portable presence.

chapters.title: A city seen from above, in 1997
chapters.body: The first Grand Theft Auto, made by DMA Design in 1997, watches the city from above the rooftops. There is no single line to follow: there are three cities: Liberty City, San Andreas, Vice City: a phone that rings, a job to take and a multiplier that climbs while the police close in. The core rule is already here: the world does not wait for the player, it keeps going, and the player decides how much noise to make crossing it.

chapters.title: When a corner can hide the street
chapters.body: In 2001 GTA III lowers the view between the buildings of Liberty City. It looks like a camera change; it is a change of game. From above, the map was a plane readable at a glance; from the ground it becomes a route to memorise. The protagonist stays silent, and that silence lets the city, the radio and the encounters speak. From here the series stops telling a heist and starts telling a place.

chapters.title: Vice City, 1986 in neon
chapters.body: Vice City, in 2002, gives the series a voice and a decade. Tommy Vercetti speaks, and around him the eighties city is not a backdrop but a soundtrack: the radio stations set the tone of every drive, and changing frequency changes the genre of the scene being crossed. This is where GTA understands that a setting is not a graphic theme but an edit.

chapters.title: Distance enters the story
chapters.body: San Andreas, in 2004, does not add a city: it adds the space between cities. Between Los Santos, San Fierro and Las Venturas lie countryside, desert and hours of road, and travel stops being an interval between two missions. The protagonist also changes over time: stamina, driving, appearance: so the length of the playthrough becomes visible on him.

chapters.title: A small console, a large decision
chapters.body: In 2009 Chinatown Wars takes the series to the Nintendo DS and, rather than compressing a three-dimensional GTA, looks at Liberty City from above again: this time with a tilted camera that rotates. The touch screen is not ornament: it turns a screwdriver, forces a junction box, handles goods. It is the proof that the identity of the series was never the perspective, but the relation between map, haste and consequence.

game.Name: Grand Theft Auto: Chinatown Wars
game.Overview: Grand Theft Auto: Chinatown Wars is an entirely original entry into the critically acclaimed Grand Theft Auto series, and brings a new level of interactivity to its sprawling open environments. With the use of the DS touch screen, players navigate their way through the streets as they uncover the truth behind an epic tale of crime and corruption within the Triad crime syndicate, delivering the unprecedented amount of depth that has become a true trademark of the franchise.

chapters.title: Switching character like switching shot
chapters.body: GTA V, in 2013, keeps three protagonists running at once and lets the player move between them. Michael, Franklin and Trevor do not alternate for variety: during a heist the switch works as a cut, and the same scene is seen from three positions and three temperaments. Los Santos, meanwhile, keeps living where nobody is watching.

chapters.title: What grew around the series
chapters.body: A few weeks after GTA V, in 2013, Los Santos reopened as a shared mode: not a new entry, but the same place left running. From there the map kept changing for years, and people did things in it nobody had designed: up to shooting an entire film inside it, a 2024 documentary in which two actors without a stage try to put on Hamlet. It is the most precise measure of how habitable that city became.
